# The Error in the Meter

A meter is the distance light travels through a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. That is the official definition, and the first thing to notice about it is how ugly the number is. Nobody designing a system from scratch would choose it. It was chosen in 1983 because a meter already existed, and the new definition had to match the old one as closely as anyone could tell. The old one was a count of wavelengths of krypton light, fixed in 1960 to match a platinum-iridium bar in a vault outside Paris. That bar was cast in 1889 to match an older platinum bar finished in 1799, and the 1799 bar was made to match the Earth.

Or it was supposed to. The story of how it failed to, and of what that failure did to the man who believed himself responsible, is one of my favorite stories in the history of science. I think it is really about a question that sounds simple and isn't: what does it mean to get something wrong?

## The measure of all things

Start with the problem the meter was meant to solve. France before the Revolution had no system of measurement in any sense we would recognize. By one modern estimate it had some 250,000 local units going by about 800 names. A pint in one town was not a pint in the next. Cloth was sold by an ell that varied with the city and sometimes with the cloth. Land was often measured by the amount of work it took to plow or the amount of seed it took to sow, which was sensible for a peasant and hopeless for a tax assessor. Every measure was a local custom, guarded by local interests and opaque to outsiders, and that opacity was partly the point.

The revolutionaries wanted to sweep this away, and they wanted the replacement to be beyond argument. A unit based on the king's foot would be arbitrary, and a unit based on Paris custom would be an imposition. So the Academy of Sciences proposed taking the unit from nature itself. The meter would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured along the meridian that ran through Paris. No nation owned the Earth. Condorcet supplied the motto: a measure "for all time, for all people."

There was a simpler option on the table, the length of a pendulum that swings once per second. It comes out close to a meter and can be reproduced in any decent laboratory. The Academy rejected it, partly for defensible reasons (it depends on the definition of the second, and it varies with latitude) and partly, one suspects, because measuring the planet was the grander project and the savants had a splendid new instrument they wanted to use.

Nobody could survey the whole quadrant, so the plan was to measure a piece of it and extrapolate. The piece ran from Dunkirk on the Channel to Barcelona on the Mediterranean. The method was to lay a chain of triangles down the length of France, sighting from steeple to hilltop to tower, and to fix the latitude of each end by the stars. Two astronomers were sent out in June 1792. Jean-Baptiste Delambre took the northern stretch and Pierre Méchain took the southern. It was expected to take about a year, and it took seven.

## Two astronomers

The timing could hardly have been worse. Within weeks of their departure the monarchy fell, and France was soon at war with most of Europe. Delambre spent the following months being arrested. A stranger who climbed church towers with brass instruments and hung signals on hilltops looked like a spy to every village militia between Paris and the coast. It did not help that the signals were made of white cloth, since white was the royalist color. He was hauled before crowds and made to explain geodesy to people who were deciding whether to let him go. His passes were signed by a government that kept ceasing to exist. He was eventually purged from the project altogether during the Terror and reinstated only after it ended. Through all of this he kept measuring, cheerfully and methodically, and recorded everything in bound notebooks in ink.

Méchain's trouble was of a different kind. He was by every account one of the most meticulous observers alive, a man who had found comets by patience and whose results colleagues trusted without checking. He worked quickly at first, carrying his triangles across the Pyrenees and fixing the latitude of his southern endpoint, the fortress of Montjuïc above Barcelona, from thousands of star observations. Then a series of misfortunes hit. He was badly injured helping a friend demonstrate a pump, when a lever caught him in the chest and left his right arm weak for the rest of his life. France and Spain went to war, and he became an enemy alien, kept in Barcelona and barred from the fortress.

With nothing else to do during the winter of 1793–94, he did what a conscientious man would. He set up his instrument at his inn in the city and measured the latitude again, as a check. The inn lay a short, known distance from Montjuïc, so the two latitudes should have differed by a known amount. They missed it by a little more than three seconds of arc.

Three arcseconds of latitude is about a hundred meters on the ground. Set against the whole meridian arc it was small, and it would have changed the final meter by a sliver. But Méchain's results did not usually disagree with themselves by three seconds. He had two answers of the highest quality that could not both be right, and he could not go back to the fortress to find out which was wrong.

He told no one.

## The secret

What followed was a ten-year collapse. Méchain reported the Montjuïc result and suppressed the one from the inn. He left Spain for Italy and lingered there for months, finding reasons not to come home. Back in France, he dragged out his remaining triangles for years, working in the mountains of the south while Delambre finished the north and came down to meet him. His letters from the period are full of self-reproach that his colleagues could not interpret, because they did not know what he was reproaching himself for. When an international commission met in Paris to compute the final meter, he delivered tidy summaries of his data and refused to hand over the original records.

The commission did its sums, the platinum bar was made, and in 1799 it was presented to the legislature with considerable ceremony. Méchain was honored and made director of the Paris Observatory, and he remained miserable. He began lobbying to extend the survey south to the Balearic Islands. The stated reason was scientific. The private one was that a new southern endpoint would make the Barcelona latitude irrelevant and bury his discrepancy for good. He got his expedition, went back to Spain, caught a fever in the coastal marshes, and died there in 1804.

His papers went to Delambre, who was writing the official account of the survey. Delambre found a mess of loose sheets and scraps, and as he worked through them he found the secret. The second latitude was there. So was evidence that Méchain had tidied his records, recopying and adjusting them so that his observations looked more consistent than they had been. He had invented nothing. He had smoothed real results, in the manner of a man who could not stand to let anyone see the scatter.

Delambre then made a decision that I find interesting, though I'm not sure it was right. He published an account that told the public what it needed to know, with the discrepancy mentioned and the anguish and the retouching left out. He deposited the papers in the Observatory archives, where anyone determined could find them. He protected his colleague's reputation and left the evidence intact.

## What the error was

The historian Ken Alder told this story in *The Measure of All Things*, and the part of it that has stayed with me is the argument that Méchain was in some sense not wrong at all.

A generation later, an astronomer named Nicollet reanalyzed the Barcelona data. He found that if the stars passing north of the zenith were grouped separately from those passing south and the two groups were balanced against each other, most of the discrepancy vanished. Méchain's instrument had probably had a slight consistent bias, the kind that shifts every reading the same way. His individual observations were superb and agreed with one another beautifully. They were all slightly off in the same direction, and the direction depended on where in the sky he pointed.

Today that is a textbook distinction between precision and accuracy, between random error and systematic error. In 1794 the distinction did not exist in any usable form, and neither did the idea beneath it, that error is a natural property of measurement which can be studied, modeled and managed like any other phenomenon. An observer of Méchain's generation treated his results as something like his word of honor. A good astronomer used judgment to select his best observations and presented those. Discordant data meant that he had been careless. No public, agreed procedure existed for taking a pile of measurements that disagreed and extracting the best answer along with an honest statement of how far to trust it.

That procedure arrived almost as he was dying, and it grew largely out of geodesy and astronomy and their piles of inconsistent data. In 1805 Legendre, who had served on the commission that calculated the meter, published the method of least squares, a rule for combining discordant observations into the single result that fits them best. Gauss, who said he had been using the method for years, soon tied it to a theory of how errors distribute themselves, the bell curve. Laplace supplied the deeper mathematics. Within a few decades the practice of science had changed. A measurement became a value with an uncertainty attached, and stating the uncertainty became the mark of competence. Scatter in the data stopped being shameful and became information.

Méchain had treated a problem of statistics as a problem of character, mostly because nobody had yet offered him another way to see it. He spent ten years hiding something that a scientist twenty years younger would have put in a table.

## The lumpy Earth

There is a second irony. The survey was meant to tie the meter to the size of the Earth, and it showed that the Earth would not cooperate.

Extrapolating from an arc to a quadrant requires knowing the planet's shape, specifically how much it flattens toward the poles. The savants expected their own data to give them that figure. The data gave them an absurd one instead, suggesting a flattening about twice what other surveys had found. The Earth, it turned out, is not a smooth ellipsoid. It is lumpy and irregular, each meridian is slightly different from the next, and no single arc can stand for the whole. To get a usable figure, the commission had to combine the French arc with a survey done in Peru sixty years earlier, which rather undermined the premise.

The result is that the meter is wrong by its own definition. The distance from pole to equator is about 10,002,000 meters, and the bar came out roughly a fifth of a millimeter short. There is a further twist. Before the expedition, the government had issued a provisional meter calculated from older surveys. By some reckonings that provisional meter was closer to the ideal than the definitive one that took seven years, a war and one man's sanity to produce.

None of this mattered, because of what happened once the bar existed: the bar was the meter. Nobody was ever going to re-survey France to check a ruler. Scientists understood within a few years that the tie to the Earth was approximate, and they left the standard alone, because consistency in a standard matters far more than conformity to a meridian. Its value lies in the fact that everyone's copy agrees with everyone else's. The appeal to nature had served mostly as rhetoric, a way of giving the unit an authority that no king or city could claim. The meter was a convention that presented itself as a discovery.

The convention took a long time to stick. The French public hated the new measures and ignored them, Napoleon let the old names back in, and the metric system did not become compulsory in France until 1840. But it spread because a shared arbitrary unit beats a quarter of a million local ones, and in 1875 the nations that had adopted it signed a treaty to maintain it jointly. The new international bar of 1889 was built to match the old French bar and made no reference to the Earth.

Since then the meter has been redefined twice, each time in terms of something more stable and more universal than a bar: first a wavelength of light, then the speed of light itself. In 2019 the kilogram followed, the last unit to give up its physical artifact. Condorcet's ambition has been met better than he could have imagined. The units really are available to all people for all time, and anyone with the right equipment can reproduce them without visiting a vault. Yet every redefinition was tuned to preserve the previous one. That is where the 299,792,458 comes from. The number carries, in its digits, the size of a platinum bar made in 1799, including the fifth of a millimeter by which the bar missed the Earth. Somewhere in that shortfall is the small contribution of a three-arcsecond discrepancy measured from the terrace of an inn in Barcelona.

## What I take from it

I come back to this story because I think Méchain's mistake is easy to repeat. I don't mean the instrumental bias, which was nobody's fault. I mean the decision to smooth the record.

He believed his job was to be right. On that view a discrepancy is a kind of confession, and the natural thing to do with it is hide it, round it off, and present the answer that looks the way a correct answer should. The view that replaced his holds that the job is to say what you found and how far to trust it. On that view the discrepancy is the most valuable thing in the notebook, because it shows where your understanding runs out. As it happened, the scatter Méchain hid was evidence of a real effect, one that a later analyst could diagnose only because Delambre had kept the raw papers.

I feel the pull of Méchain's view myself. A clean answer looks more competent than a hedged one, and when a confident sentence and an honest one diverge, the confident sentence is the easier one to write. What I take from the meter is that the tidied answer does more harm than the honest one. Delambre's inked notebooks, with all their visible mess, served science better than Méchain's recopied pages. A standard that was slightly wrong and openly agreed on served the world better than a perfect one would have, had there been such a thing to find.

Méchain died thinking he had spoiled a measure meant for all time. In fact his error survives inside a unit that works perfectly well, and the discrepancy that tormented him belongs to the early history of the tools that would have set his mind at rest. I find that consoling, though I'd much rather he had been able to write it down and let it go.
